fixes.explanation: That cry belongs to someone else. Bartimaeus, a blind beggar, cried out to Jesus as the Son of David and asked Him for mercy (Mark 10:47). Thomas says something different here, “My Lord and my God!” Same Jesus, different moment.
Close, but the text says something different. The doors are locked for fear of the Jews, and still “…Jesus came and stood among them.” Locked doors and all, He is right there with them.
No scroll comes out in this scene, friend. The text says Jesus shows them His hands and His side. I'd guess nobody in that room was thinking about reading material.

Yes, they rejoiced! The text says the disciples rejoiced when they saw the Lord. They were together with the doors locked for fear of the Jews, and then they saw Him and rejoiced. I think that joy changed the whole feel of that room.
That's not the word, friend. The text says the disciples rejoiced when they saw the Lord. That comes right after He shows them His hands and His side. It's a joyful moment.
Almost, but He says something different. Right after the second greeting of peace, Jesus says, “As the Father has sent Me, so also I am sending you.” His words are about sending, not about hiding.

Exactly right. Right after the second greeting of peace, Jesus says, “As the Father has sent Me, so also I am sending you.” That's about sending, and the text gives no word about staying hidden. I think that was quite a thing to hear with the doors locked.

That's not the word Jesus uses, friend. He says, “If you forgive anyone his sins, they are forgiven…” Swapping in “remembered” would turn the whole sentence upside down. Give me forgiven any day, and I bet the disciples felt the same.

Not this time, friend. The other disciples tell Thomas, one of the Twelve, “We have seen the Lord!” But he replies, “Unless I see the nail marks in His hands, and put my finger where the nails have been, and put my hand into His side, I will never believe.” So he doesn't believe right away, and he asks to see and to touch.

That's it. Thomas, one of the Twelve, hears the other disciples say, “We have seen the Lord!” But he replies, “Unless I see the nail marks in His hands, and put my finger where the nails have been, and put my hand into His side, I will never believe.” His answer comes with conditions about seeing and touching.

You've got it. Thomas says, “Unless I see the nail marks in His hands, and put my finger where the nails have been, and put my hand into His side, I will never believe.” That's a long order, friend, with seeing and touching both on it. I think Thomas had thought it all the way through.
Waiting isn't the word here. The meeting with Thomas comes eight days later, but Jesus doesn't tell him to wait. He says, “Stop doubting and believe.”

Jesus says something different. He tells Thomas, “Because you have seen Me, you have believed; blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed.” The ones He calls blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed. That's the group He names, friend.
